Most towns and cities have a central shopping area called the town centre, and undercover shopping centres are common. Most shops are open seven days a week, with reduced hours on Sundays and public holidays. Many towns have markets one or more days a week.

Pubs are an important part of social culture; most communities have a ‘local’. Pub quizzes, pool and darts are popular. You must be 18 to buy alcohol; under-18s may be allowed in some pubs with an adult. At 16 you can drink wine or beer with a meal in a hotel or restaurant if with someone over 18. Pubs usually open from 11am (12 noon on Sundays); the licensee decides opening hours.

You must be 18 to enter betting shops or gambling clubs. There are casinos in many places. The National Lottery has weekly draws (tickets or scratch cards). Players must be 18 or over (the minimum age rose from 16 to 18 in April 2021).

It is against the law to treat a pet cruelly or neglect it. All dogs in public places must wear a collar showing the owner’s name and address. Owners must keep dogs under control and clean up after them. Vets provide vaccinations and treatment; charities may help people who cannot afford one.
Sites such as Facebook and Twitter are a popular way to keep in touch, organise events and share photos, videos and opinions, often on mobile phones.
Many people enjoy cooking and invite each other for dinner. A wide variety of food is eaten thanks to the UK’s rich cultural heritage and diverse population.

Film, comedy, TV and radio · Life in the UK
The UK has had a major influence on modern cinema. Films were first shown publicly here in 1896, and British film makers have been famous for special effects ever since.
Charlie Chaplin as his famous tramp character
British actors have worked in the UK and USA since the early days. Sir Charles (Charlie) Chaplin became famous in silent films for his tramp character.
British studios flourished in the 1930s: directors Sir Alexander Korda and Sir Alfred Hitchcock (who later left for Hollywood and directed until his death in 1980).
In the Second World War, films such as In Which We Serve boosted morale. Later, Sir David Lean and Ridley Scott found great success.
The 1950s and 1960s were a high point for comedies: Passport to Pimlico, The Ladykillers and the Carry On films.
Many films are now made in the UK by foreign companies using British expertise, including the two highest-grossing franchises: Harry Potter and James Bond.
Ealing Studios claims to be the oldest continuously working film studio in the world.
Britain is strong in special effects and animation: Nick Park has won four Oscars, three for Wallace and Gromit.

Places of interest · Life in the UK

A large network of public footpaths crosses the countryside, with mountain biking, mountaineering and hill walking. There are 15 national parks in England, Wales and Scotland: protected countryside everyone can visit, where people also live and work.
Museums range from small community museums to large national collections. Most landmarks are open to the public, generally for a charge.
The National Trust (England, Wales and Northern Ireland) and the National Trust for Scotland are charities that preserve important buildings, coastline and countryside.
The National Trust was founded in 1895 by three volunteers. It now has more than 61,000 volunteers.

Democracy and the constitution · Life in the UK
Chapter {#} · The UK government, the law and your role
The UK is a parliamentary democracy with the monarch as head of state. Democracy is a system where the whole adult population gets a say, by voting directly or choosing representatives.

At the turn of the 19th century only a small group could vote: men over 21 who owned a certain amount of property. The franchise (the number of people with the right to vote) grew during the 19th century, and parties began to involve ordinary men and women.

A constitution is a set of principles by which a country is governed: its institutions, how their power is kept in check, and its laws and conventions.
The British constitution is not written down in any single document, so it is called ‘unwritten’.
This is mainly because the UK, unlike America or France, never had a revolution that permanently created a totally new system. Institutions developed over hundreds of years.
Some want a single document; others think an unwritten constitution gives more flexibility and better government.
